title: Sick in body, not in mind
hookLine: an old man leaves glowing from one line he hasn't understood yet
tomorrow: a monk lies sick and alone. who finally washes him?

cards: When someone is sick, people say: get well soon, feel better, stay strong. All aimed at the body. A householder named Nakulapita came to the Buddha old, worn out and often sick, and asked for a teaching he could keep.
The Buddha gave him one line: train yourself this way, though my body is sick, my mind will not be sick. Nakulapita went away delighted, his face bright. And here is the odd part.
He hadn't asked what the line meant. So what was he so happy about, and how could it even work?

teach.h: SARIPUTTA ASKS: WHAT DOES IT MEAN?
teach.b: The sutta solves its own puzzle, through another person. On the way home, Nakulapita meets Sariputta, one of the Buddha's chief disciples, who notices his calm, bright face and asks what happened.
Nakulapita tells him the line. Did you ask what it means? says Sariputta. No.
So Sariputta explains. Someone who hasn't learned the teaching, he says, takes the body as me, as mine, as who I am.

Then when the body changes and breaks down, sorrow and despair arise; the illness spreads from the body into the mind. Someone who has learned the teaching doesn't hold the body as self. The body still changes.

teach.h: THE BODY ACHES; THE MIND ISN'T DRAGGED.
teach.b: But the mind isn't dragged down with it. That's the answer to the puzzle. The line was never a promise that the body would heal, and it wasn't a trick of positive thinking.

The body is allowed to be sick. The mind trains not to add I am this sickness on top. And notice what made Nakulapita glow before he understood any of it: being told that his mind had a job to do, even now, old and ill.
Here's a detail worth passing on: the sutta's wisest explanation came not from the Buddha but from a friend on the road who asked the right question.

how: Buddhists who are ill often use reflection and mindfulness alongside medical care, and some keep the line from this sutta as a training phrase during sickness.

o: a body that aches while the mind trains not to be dragged down
a sickness believed to start in the mind first
the belief that illness is punishment for past deeds

games.q: the old man and the line — tap the pairs.
p: takes the body as me and mine

s: the Buddha promised Nakulapita his body would heal
the line is a training for the mind; the body is allowed to be sick.
Sariputta, not the Buddha, explained the line in this sutta
he met Nakulapita on the way home and asked if he'd understood it.
'not sick in mind' means thinking positive thoughts
it means not taking the body as self, so illness doesn't spread into the mind.

games.q: your uncle has a bad flu and keeps saying 'i'm useless, i'm just a sick body now.' what does the sutta suggest?
o: tell him to cheer up and think positive until he heals.
the body is sick; he isn't only his body. his mind can still rest.
agree, but remind him it won't last forever.
games.why: Sariputta explains: taking the body as self lets illness drag the mind down. the body can be sick without the mind being sick.

practice: Notice one ache or tired place in your body, small or large. Say quietly, out loud if you can: the body aches; the mind can rest. Repeat it slowly with the breath, letting the ache be there without making it who you are.
If the ache shifts or fades, let that be fine too.

wordCard.voice: Sick in body: the body allowed to ache and change, while the mind trains not to take the illness as who it is.

carryVoice: Keep this close: not sick in mind, even when the body is. Three of nine.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 22.1 (Nakulapita Sutta: the old, sick householder; 'though I am sick in body, my mind will not be sick'; Sariputta explains how the uninstructed take form as self and the instructed do not)
